title: Number of Provinces
statement:
A country has `n` cities, numbered `0` to `n - 1`. The `n x n` matrix `isConnected` describes the roads between them: `isConnected[i][j]` is `1` when cities `i` and `j` are joined directly and `0` when they are not. The matrix is symmetric, and every city counts as joined to itself.

Two cities lie in the same **province** when you can travel from one to the other along direct links, possibly passing through other cities. A province is a largest group of cities linked this way, so every city belongs to exactly one province. Return the number of provinces.
notes:
## Intuition

Read the matrix as a graph: cities are nodes and each `1` off the diagonal is an edge. A province is then a connected component, so the task is to count components. A flood fill does exactly that: start a depth-first search from any city nobody has reached yet, mark everything it can reach, and count one province for each such start. (Union-find counts the same thing: start with `n` groups and subtract one whenever a link merges two different groups.)

## Approach

1. Keep a `visited` flag for every city and a counter `provinces`.
2. `dfs(city)` marks `city` and recurses into every `other` city it is linked to that is not yet visited.
3. Scan the cities in order. Each unvisited `city` begins a new province: add 1 to `provinces` and call `dfs(city)` to mark its whole province.
4. Return `provinces`.

## Example 1, step by step

`isConnected = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]]`. City `0` is unvisited, so `provinces = 1` and `dfs(0)` marks `0`, sees the link to `1` and marks `1` (city `2` is not linked). City `1` is already visited, so it is skipped. City `2` is unvisited: `provinces = 2` and `dfs(2)` marks only itself. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every city is visited once and its row of `n` entries is scanned once.
- Space: O(n) for `visited` and the recursion stack.

## Pitfalls

- Mark a city as visited before recursing into its neighbours, or two linked cities call each other forever.
- Count a province only when the outer loop finds an unvisited city, not inside `dfs`.
- The diagonal is always `1`; it is harmless because the city is already visited when its own row is scanned.
- Cities can share a province only through others (`0–1–2` with no direct `0–2` link). Looking only at a city's direct neighbours, without searching onward, splits such a province in two.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of cities |
| `visited` | `visited[c]` is true once city `c` has been reached |
| `provinces` | number of provinces found so far |
| `city` | the city being started from (outer loop) or explored (in `dfs`) |
| `other` | a city that may be directly linked to `city` |

narration.3: No city has been reached yet.
narration.4: Count provinces as new flood fills start.
narration.6: dfs marks every city reachable from city.
narration.7: Mark first, so a linked city never sends the search back here.
narration.8: Look along this city's row at every other city.
narration.9: A direct link to a city not yet reached...
narration.10: ...belongs to the same province: explore it too.
narration.16: An unvisited city is not in any province found so far.
narration.17: So it starts a new province.
narration.18: Flood its whole province so none of its cities is counted again.
narration.21: Every city now belongs to a counted province.
